Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN)  -- Zimbabwe police arrested on Friday a magistrate who ordered the release of a senior opposition politician granted bail by the country's High Court, a lawyer said. A Zimbabwean policeman patrols outside the entrance of Mutare Magistrates court. The order to release the politician had been suspended when state lawyers appealed the HIgh Court decision. Trust Maanda, a lawyer in Mutare city about 300 kilometers (186 miles) east of Harare, told CNN by phone that magistrate Livingstone Chipadze had been arrested. "He is in police custody. The police are saying he ordered the release of Roy Bennett in compliance with the High Court ruling," said Maanda. Bennett is the choice of the opposition Movement for Democratic Change (MDC) for deputy agriculture minister under the power-sharing government formed last month. On Wednesday, Chipadze ordered Bennett be released from a prison in Mutare as had been ruled by the High Court last week. However, that order, which required Bennett to post $2,000 as bail, was suspended after the state filed an appeal with Zimbabwe's Supreme Court. "I can confirm the arrest, but I will be in position to tell you the charge he will face later," said a police official in Mutare over the phone. "He is likely to go to court on Saturday or Monday. But most magistrates here [in Mutare] have gone on strike over his arrest." Chipadze joins Bennett in prison in Mutare. Bennett was arrested on February 13 and is facing charges of possessing arms for the purposes of banditry, terrorism and sabotage. The continued detention of Bennett, an ally of MDC leader and Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai, is seen by many as a crack in the foundation of the coalition Tsvangirai formed with President Robert Mugabe. Meanwhile, a Zimbabwe High Court judge Friday ordered the immediate release of three human rights activists in state "safe custody" to testify against human rights activist Jestina Mukoko, who is facing charges of plotting to topple Mugabe. Opposition MDC activists Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa and Terry Musona have been missing since October last year after they were abducted from their homes under the cover of darkness. Lawyers Chris Mhike and Innocent Chagonda took the state to the High Court in an attempt to win the release the trio. But the state represented by Nelson Mutsonziwa had opposed the application, saying the three would be state witnesses when the trial of Mukoko starts. The MDC lawyers then successfully argued that the three were bread winners for their families and the state had not provided their families with assistance while they are in custody. Delivering the judgment, Justice Ben Hlatswayo said, "I order the immediate release of Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa and Terry Musona from police custody or the custody of any other state agent. This order stands enforceable notwithstanding the noting or filing of an appeal." Relatives of the three who were milling around the High Court could not hide their joy after Mhike told them of Hlatswayo's ruling.

A Zimbabwean police officer was seen guarding the entrance to the Magistrates Court in Mutare.

Trust Maanda, an attorney in Mutare, roughly 300 kilometers (186 miles) east of Harare, told CNN by telephone that Magistrate Livingstone Chipadze had been taken into custody.

“He is in police custody. The police are saying he ordered the release of Roy Bennett in compliance with the High Court ruling,” Maanda said.

Bennett is the Movement for Democratic Change’s choice to serve as deputy agriculture minister in the power-sharing administration established last month.

Chipadze on Wednesday instructed officials to release Bennett from a Mutare prison, following a High Court decision issued the previous week. The ruling granted Bennett bail of $2,000. However, its implementation had been halted after government lawyers appealed to Zimbabwe’s Supreme Court.

A Mutare police official confirmed Chipadze’s arrest by telephone but said the specific charge would be disclosed later.

“He is likely to go to court on Saturday or Monday. But most magistrates here [in Mutare] have gone on strike over his arrest,” the official said.

Chipadze is now being held in the same Mutare prison as Bennett.

Bennett was detained on February 13 and accused of possessing weapons for use in banditry, terrorism and sabotage. Many view his continued imprisonment as evidence of strain within the coalition between MDC leader and Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai and President Robert Mugabe. Bennett is an ally of Tsvangirai.

In a separate development Friday, a Zimbabwean High Court judge ordered the immediate release of three human rights activists being held in state “safe custody” so they could testify against activist Jestina Mukoko. Mukoko faces allegations that she plotted to overthrow Mugabe.

MDC activists Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa and Terry Musona had not been seen since October of the previous year, when they were taken from their homes at night.

Attorneys Chris Mhike and Innocent Chagonda went to the High Court seeking the trio’s release. Nelson Mutsonziwa, representing the state, opposed their request, arguing that the three were intended to testify for the prosecution when Mukoko’s trial began.

The MDC lawyers countered successfully that Tembo, Tarumbwa and Musona supported their families financially and that the government had provided no help to those families while the three remained detained.

Issuing his decision, Justice Ben Hlatswayo stated: “I order the immediate release of Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa and Terry Musona from police custody or the custody of any other state agent. This order stands enforceable notwithstanding the noting or filing of an appeal.”

Relatives gathered around the High Court openly celebrated after Mhike informed them of Hlatswayo’s decision.

Magistrate Livingstone Chipadze was taken into custody after directing prison officials to release Bennett on bail. Authorities accused Chipadze of improperly handling the release order, according to reports from Zimbabwe.

counterfactuals.output:
**Zimbabwe crisis deepens as Bennett remains detained, magistrate arrested and High Court orders activists freed**

*The confrontation poses an early test for Zimbabwe’s new unity government and raises fresh concerns about the rule of law.*

**HARARE, Zimbabwe, Feb. 18, 2009** — Zimbabwe’s fragile power-sharing government was plunged into a deepening political and judicial crisis Wednesday as opposition politician Roy Bennett remained in custody, authorities arrested the magistrate who had ordered his release, and the High Court directed the government to free three activists who had disappeared before turning up in state detention.

Bennett, a senior figure in Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai’s Movement for Democratic Change, was arrested on Feb. 13 — the day the new cabinet was sworn in — after returning to Zimbabwe to take up the post of deputy agriculture minister.

His detention has become the first major confrontation between the MDC and the security establishment still dominated by President Robert Mugabe and his ZANU-PF party. It has also intensified doubts over whether the unity government, formed after months of disputed elections and political violence, can function while police, intelligence agencies and prosecutors continue to pursue opposition figures.

Bennett was initially accused of treason, although prosecutors later pursued allegations involving weapons and plans to commit sabotage, banditry or terrorism. He has denied wrongdoing, and the MDC says the case is politically motivated.

A magistrate in the eastern city of Mutare, Livingstone Chipadze, granted Bennett bail and ordered his release. But prison officials did not immediately comply after prosecutors invoked legal procedures intended to suspend a bail order while the state considers an appeal.

Chipadze was subsequently arrested on allegations of criminal abuse of office over his handling of Bennett’s case. His arrest sent a stark warning through Zimbabwe’s legal community and prompted accusations that judicial officers were being punished for issuing decisions unfavorable to the government.

Lawyers and opposition officials said the sequence of events — a release order, continued detention and then the arrest of the magistrate — demonstrated that elements of the state were prepared to disregard or intimidate the courts.

The government has maintained that Bennett faces legitimate criminal allegations and that prosecutors are acting within the law. No conviction has been entered against him.

### High Court orders three detainees freed

In a separate but closely related development, the High Court ordered the release of three men linked to the MDC who had been missing for weeks before their eventual appearance in police custody.

The three — MDC members Gandhi Mudzingwa and Kisimusi Dhlamini, and freelance journalist Andrison Manyere — were among a group of activists and opposition supporters abducted from their homes or seized by unidentified men during late 2008. For weeks, officials denied knowing where they were.

They later appeared in state custody and were accused of involvement in an alleged campaign of bombings and insurgency against the Mugabe government. The detainees and their lawyers said they had been abducted, held incommunicado and tortured. The state denied sanctioning torture and said the suspects were connected to criminal plots.

The High Court ruled that the three could not continue to be held unlawfully and ordered their release. Lawyers, however, remained cautious, noting that Zimbabwean authorities have repeatedly delayed or resisted implementing court orders in politically sensitive cases.

The ruling added to pressure on the government to explain the disappearance and treatment of opposition activists. Human-rights organizations say the abductions formed part of a coordinated campaign to weaken the MDC before and during negotiations over the unity administration.

### First major test for Tsvangirai

Tsvangirai was sworn in as prime minister on Feb. 11 under a power-sharing agreement intended to end nearly a year of political turmoil following Zimbabwe’s disputed 2008 elections.

The arrangement left Mugabe as president while bringing Tsvangirai and other MDC officials into government. Cabinet ministries were divided between ZANU-PF and the two MDC formations, but control of the security services remained a central point of contention.

Bennett’s arrest just two days after Tsvangirai took office underscored the limits of the prime minister’s authority. Although Bennett had been selected by the MDC to serve as deputy agriculture minister, he was detained before he could be sworn in.

The MDC called for his immediate release and demanded that all political prisoners and abducted activists be freed. Party officials warned that the continued detention of opposition members violated both the spirit and the terms of the power-sharing agreement.

Tsvangirai now faces a difficult choice: remain in the coalition in the hope of gradually reforming state institutions, or confront Mugabe over actions that many MDC supporters view as evidence that repression is continuing under the cover of national unity.

The crisis comes as Zimbabwe struggles with economic collapse, severe food shortages, hyperinflation and a cholera epidemic. Foreign governments and donors have said substantial financial assistance will depend on evidence that the new administration respects human rights, restores the rule of law and implements genuine political reforms.

The arrest of a judicial officer for granting bail, coupled with resistance to court-ordered releases, is likely to reinforce international concerns that the unity government has not yet established effective civilian or legal control over Zimbabwe’s security apparatus.

For the moment, the three cases have converged into a single test: whether court orders will be obeyed and whether the MDC’s entry into government has brought any real change to the treatment of political opponents.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the legal and political tensions surrounding Zimbabwe’s new power-sharing government between Morgan Tsvangirai and Robert Mugabe, using quotes from lawyers, police officials, and court judgments.
counterfactuals.output:
## Zimbabwe’s unity government strained by arrests, disputed authority and defiance of courts

Zimbabwe’s power-sharing government, formed in February 2009 by President Robert Mugabe and Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai, was intended to end the violence and institutional paralysis that followed the disputed 2008 elections. Instead, its first months exposed a continuing struggle over control of the police, prosecutors, courts and security services.

Under the Global Political Agreement, Mugabe remained president while Tsvangirai became prime minister. Cabinet posts were divided among Mugabe’s ZANU-PF, Tsvangirai’s Movement for Democratic Change and a smaller MDC faction. Yet key coercive institutions—notably the police, army, intelligence service and attorney-general’s office—remained dominated by Mugabe loyalists.

### Roy Bennett’s arrest

The sharpest early confrontation concerned Roy Bennett, Tsvangirai’s choice for deputy agriculture minister. Police arrested Bennett on 13 February 2009, the day the new cabinet was sworn in.

Police spokesman Wayne Bvudzijena said Bennett faced allegations of **“attempting to commit acts of insurgency, banditry, sabotage or terrorism.”** The state later pursued weapons and terrorism-related charges based largely on claims involving an alleged plot several years earlier.

Bennett’s lawyers argued that the prosecution was politically motivated and that officials repeatedly frustrated bail orders. Attorney Beatrice Mtetwa described the authorities’ conduct as an effort to keep him imprisoned regardless of what the courts decided. After a High Court judge granted bail, the prosecution invoked appeal procedures to delay his release.

The dispute became a test of whether court orders had practical force. In ordering that Bennett be freed, the High Court treated his continued confinement after bail as **“unlawful.”** The Supreme Court subsequently upheld his right to bail. Bennett was eventually released in March, but Mugabe refused to swear him into office, leaving a senior unity-government appointment unresolved.

The case showed the limits of Tsvangirai’s authority: he could nominate a minister, but could not compel Mugabe to appoint him or prevent the police and attorney-general from prosecuting him.

### Abductions and political detainees

The government also inherited cases involving opposition activists and human-rights campaigners abducted before the coalition took office. Among the most prominent was Jestina Mukoko, director of the Zimbabwe Peace Project, who was seized from her home in December 2008 and held incommunicado before appearing in police custody.

Mukoko said state agents tortured her and forced her to participate in interrogations and staged recordings. Her lawyers maintained that her disappearance, secret detention and mistreatment made a fair prosecution impossible.

Police officials denied responsibility for the initial abduction, saying she came into lawful custody only later. That distinction was rejected as implausible by human-rights lawyers, who noted that the authorities sought to prosecute her using information allegedly obtained during the secret detention.

In **Jestina Mukoko v Attorney-General**, the Supreme Court found that her constitutional protections had been violated, including her rights to personal liberty, freedom from torture and the protection of the law. It ordered:

> **“The State is permanently stayed from prosecuting the applicant.”**

The judgment was important because it did more than release Mukoko: it barred the prosecution altogether on the ground that state misconduct had undermined the judicial process. The court found violations of sections 13, 15 and 18 of the former Constitution, covering unlawful detention, torture or inhuman treatment, and fair legal protection.

### Lawyers challenge police conduct

Defence lawyers repeatedly complained that police officers ignored judicial orders, denied access to clients and moved detainees between facilities to frustrate legal applications. Lawyers including Mtetwa and Alec Muchadehama argued that the central issue was no longer simply whether individual defendants qualified for bail, but whether the executive accepted the courts’ authority.

Muchadehama himself was arrested in May 2009 after helping secure the release of political detainees. The prosecution accused him of improperly causing detainees to be freed, while fellow lawyers said he had merely implemented valid court orders. The episode deepened concern that lawyers could be punished for insisting that judicial decisions be obeyed.

The Law Society of Zimbabwe and other legal groups described such arrests as an attack on the profession and on the rule of law. Their criticism focused on a recurring pattern: a court would grant bail or order release, prosecutors would appeal or police would delay compliance, and the detainee would remain in custody.

### A political agreement without unified control

The legal conflicts reflected unresolved political questions within the coalition:

- **Security services:** senior commanders had long declared their loyalty to Mugabe and ZANU-PF, not to an MDC-led political transition.
- **Attorney-general:** Mugabe’s unilateral appointment of Johannes Tomana was disputed by the MDC, which said senior appointments required consultation under the power-sharing agreement.
- **Reserve Bank:** the MDC similarly challenged the reappointment of central-bank governor Gideon Gono.
- **Provincial governors and diplomats:** the parties disagreed over how these posts should be distributed.
- **Farm occupations and political violence:** MDC officials said attacks and seizures continued despite the coalition’s promise to restore legality.

Mugabe and ZANU-PF portrayed the prosecutions as ordinary criminal matters and rejected demands that suspects be released merely because they were MDC members. Police officials likewise insisted that they were enforcing the law rather than undermining the coalition.

Tsvangirai, however, was under pressure from his supporters to obtain the release of detainees and halt politically selective prosecutions. His dilemma was that openly confronting Mugabe risked collapsing a government on which Zimbabwe’s economic recovery depended, while accepting continued arrests risked making the MDC appear powerless.

### Conclusion

The early unity government created a cabinet shared by former rivals but did not create a genuinely shared state. Mugabe retained decisive influence over the institutions capable of arresting, prosecuting and intimidating opponents. Tsvangirai gained formal executive office but had limited control over those institutions.

Court rulings in the Bennett and Mukoko cases demonstrated that judges could still declare detention unlawful and condemn constitutional violations. The repeated need for such orders—and the resistance to carrying them out—showed the deeper problem: Zimbabwe’s crisis was not only about the wording of its power-sharing agreement, but about whether police, prosecutors and political leaders would accept legal limits on their power.

Chipadze was accused of criminal abuse of office in connection with his handling of Bennett’s bail application, according to lawyers. The arrest raised fresh concerns among legal and human rights groups about political pressure on Zimbabwe’s judiciary.

Bennett, the Movement for Democratic Change’s treasurer and its nominee for deputy agriculture minister, was detained shortly before the formation of a unity government between President Robert Mugabe and Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai. Prosecutors have linked him to an alleged plot involving weapons and acts of insurgency, accusations Bennett and the MDC deny.

Although Chipadze ordered Bennett released on bail, the state invoked legal provisions suspending the ruling and lodged an appeal, keeping the former commercial farmer in custody while the challenge was considered. The MDC said the prosecution was politically motivated and threatened cooperation in the coalition government.

In a separate case, High Court Justice Ben Hlatshwayo ordered the immediate release of three detainees associated with opposition and human rights work: Gandhi Mudzingwa, Kisimusi Dhlamini and Andrison Manyere. The three were among activists and government critics whose detention had drawn international condemnation.

Hlatshwayo’s ruling added to mounting pressure on prison and police authorities to comply with court orders. Lawyers and rights organisations have repeatedly accused security agencies of delaying or ignoring judicial decisions in politically sensitive cases.

The developments underscored the fragility of Zimbabwe’s power-sharing arrangement, formed after months of negotiations following disputed elections and widespread political violence. Western governments and regional leaders have said the credibility of the new administration will depend in part on restoring judicial independence, ending politically motivated prosecutions and respecting human rights.
